About the Sports Medicine event

Sports Medicine is a Health Professions event in the HOSA secondary division. Format: testing · skills.

Ten in-depth lessons following the HOSA Sports Medicine 2026–27 test plan (prevention and wellness 30%, examination and assessment 30%, immediate and emergency care 16%, therapeutic intervention 16%, administration 8%) and every Round Two skill: anatomical landmarks, joint actions with HOSA’s maximum range-of-motion values, and ankle, Achilles, shoulder spica and wrist/hand taping. Built around Prentice, France and Beam, with landmark and ligament matching, ROM tables and spelling drills, special-test sorting, emergency scenarios and step-ordering for every taping sheet. Bring your own tape and pads, and always follow the scenario you are given.

Sports Medicine practice tests

Each test is an original, full-length simulation of the HOSA Round One written test, written to run slightly harder than the real thing. Every answer comes with an explanation and a reference.

  • Practice Test 1Full-length Round One simulation50 questions · 60 min
  • Practice Test 2Full-length Round One simulation50 questions · 60 min

What the test covers

Topic areaShare of test
Injury / Illness Prevention and Wellness Promotion30%
Examination, Evaluation, and Assessment30%

References: Beam’s Orthopedic Taping, Wrapping, Bracing, and Padding, France’s Introduction to Sports Medicine and Athletic Training, and Prentice’s The Role of the Athletic Trainer.

Sample Sports Medicine questions

1. A runner increases weekly mileage from 15 to 35 miles in two weeks and develops pain over the tibia. Which injury is most likely?

  1. Ligament sprain
  2. Muscle contusion
  3. Joint dislocation
  4. Stress fracture
Show answer

D. Stress fracture

Rapid increases in training load cause repetitive stress that outpaces bone repair. A common guideline is to increase training by no more than about 10% per week.

2. Athletic trainers practice under the direction of a physician. What document describes the care they may provide?

  1. A team roster
  2. Standing orders
  3. A practice schedule
  4. An equipment inventory
Show answer

B. Standing orders

Standing orders (or protocols) written by the team physician outline treatments the athletic trainer may provide.

3. After lightning is seen or thunder is heard, how long should athletes wait after the last strike or thunder before resuming play?

  1. 5 minutes
  2. 10 minutes
  3. 2 hours
  4. 30 minutes
Show answer

D. 30 minutes

The 30-minute rule restarts each time lightning is seen or thunder is heard. Athletes should shelter in a building or hard-topped vehicle.
